name: fastcpp::str::parse_u64 / u64_to_chars (developer source)
workload: bench/bench_doing_less.cpp parses 20,000 uint64 values from decimal text (fastcpp::str::parse_u64, SWAR 8-digit-word decode) and formats 20,000 uint64 values to decimal text (fastcpp::str::u64_to_chars, 2-digit table), single-threaded, minimum-of-7-samples timing.
claimed_speedup: parse_u64: 2.98x vs strtoull (12.306ns vs 36.713ns), 1.49x vs std::from_chars (18.337ns), 11.5x vs std::istringstream (141.749ns); u64_to_chars: 3.12x vs snprintf (16.624ns vs 51.83ns), 1.82x vs std::to_string (30.318ns), 7.91x vs std::ostringstream (131.548ns), but only ~1.27x vs std::to_chars (21.074ns) -- the repo's own README/results call this 'HONEST CAVEAT ... not an improvement on the standard library'
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04 / Linux 6.18, shared cloud VM
tradeoffs: parse_u64 drops locale handling, leading-whitespace skipping, base-prefix detection and errno that strtoull provides; it requires an 8-byte unaligned load per word (load_unaligned) and only accepts ASCII decimal digits, reporting overflow/non-digit input by returning consumed=0 rather than an error code. u64_to_chars needs a caller-provided 20-byte buffer and writes no NUL terminator; digit count is estimated from bit-width via a lookup table rather than computed by division.
caveats: PRIVATE repo, readable only via the authenticated gh CLI (private:developer-source), not publicly browsable -- capped at tier C rather than A despite full compiler/flags/CPU/commit metadata being stated in results/fastest.json, per instruction not to claim tier A for private code. include/fastcpp/string/parse.hpp:106, inside parse_i64 (`-static_cast<std::int64_t>(magnitude.value)`), is a signed-negation-overflow site: when the parsed magnitude equals 2^63 (i.e. the text is INT64_MIN's magnitude), negating the cast value is undefined behavior and is flagged by UBSan in CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml runs an asan+ubsan job); the single commit in this repo's history shows no fix for it. Shared cloud VM: results/fastest.json's own caveat states absolute nanoseconds are not stable across runs or CPU-clock changes -- only ratios within one row are meaningful.
found_via: seed-record pass: results/fastest.json rows 'parse_u64' and 'u64_to_chars' (run 2026-09-02-core); include/fastcpp/string/parse.hpp; include/fastcpp/string/itoa.hpp; bench/bench_doing_less.cpp

name: fastcpp::io::buffered_writer (developer source)
workload: bench/bench_doing_less.cpp writes 20,000 short lines ('line N\n') to a real file descriptor (/dev/null) through fastcpp::io::buffered_writer (64 KiB buffer, 4 total write(2) calls) versus calling write(2) once per line (40,010 syscalls total).
claimed_speedup: 67.17x faster than one write(2) per line (2.93ns vs 196.803ns per line, results/fastest.json row 'buffered_output'); reduces the syscall count from 40,010 to 4, i.e. four orders of magnitude fewer kernel entries
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04 / Linux 6.18, shared cloud VM (bench/bench_syscall.cpp additionally reports this host as 'Not affected' by Meltdown and retbleed, i.e. no KPTI/retpoline tax)
tradeoffs: Requires an explicit flush() or destructor call to guarantee bytes reach the sink (no per-write durability); the buffer is a heap allocation (std::unique_ptr<char[]>, default 64 KiB) sized once at construction; a write larger than the remaining buffer bypasses buffering and goes straight to the sink. In the same bench file, buffered_writer also beats std::ostringstream heavily for in-memory formatting, but that comparison is not the row captured in results/fastest.json.
caveats: PRIVATE repo, readable only via the authenticated gh CLI (private:developer-source), not publicly browsable -- capped at tier C rather than A despite full compiler/flags/CPU/commit metadata being stated in results/fastest.json, per instruction not to claim tier A for private code. The header's own comment history (include/fastcpp/io/buffered_writer.hpp) originally claimed 'a write(2) costs 1-3us'; bench/bench_syscall.cpp later measured a real write(64B) to /dev/null at ~112ns and a bare kernel entry (getppid) at ~100ns on this unmitigated host -- roughly an order of magnitude below the original claim, because syscall entry cost is dominated by speculative-execution mitigations (KPTI/retpoline), which this host lacks. The repository's own text is explicit that this correction does not weaken the buffered_writer result: the count reduction (40,010 -> 4 syscalls) holds regardless of the per-syscall cost, but the previously advertised per-call nanosecond saving was overstated. Shared cloud VM: results/fastest.json's own caveat states absolute nanoseconds are not stable across runs or CPU-clock changes -- only ratios within one row are meaningful.
